title: Pleasant places (Psalm 16)
hookLine: the lines are fallen to me in pleasant places
last: WHAT ARE WE, THAT YOU CARE?

lines: SOME GOT NO LAND AT ALL.
cards: In the book of Joshua, the land is handed out by lot. A surveyor goes into the hills with a long cord, and the land is measured out with ropes: this field is yours, that slope is your cousin's.
Where your lines fell, that was your share, your inheritance, for good. Some families got rich valley soil. Some got rocky hillsides.

The priestly tribe of Levi got no land at all; God told them, I am your portion. And a psalm-writer, looking at his own life, uses that picture: the measuring lines have fallen for me. And he says where they fell.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage." Just before that, he names what his share is: "The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup."
Like the Levites, his real allotment isn't a field. It's God.

teach.h: I HAVE SET THE LORD BEFORE ME.
teach.b: The psalm is honest that this is a choice of attention, not a lucky break: "I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved."
Set: placed on purpose, like a photo on your desk where you'll see it. The result is joy, even in the body: my heart is glad, my flesh will rest in hope.
Then the psalm reaches past death: you will not leave my soul in the grave.

teach.h: THE PATH OF LIFE, FULNESS OF JOY.
teach.b: And it ends: "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore." Christians have heard that ending as resurrection.
In the book of Acts, on the day of Pentecost, Peter quotes this psalm to the crowd and says it speaks of Jesus, whose body did not stay in the grave. One honest note.
The heading calls it a michtam of David, and nobody is sure what michtam means. A golden poem, a secret, an inscription: scholars have guessed. The sources don't settle it.

teach.h: THE LINES ARE FALLEN UNTO ME IN PLEASANT PLACES.
teach.b: What the psalm does say is plain: wherever the lines fell, the LORD is the portion, and the heritage is goodly.

how: Christians pray Psalm 16 in daily prayer, and some churches read it in the Easter season, following Peter's sermon in Acts 2, which hears it as a psalm of resurrection.

o: the best seats kept for guests at a feast
where life's lines fall, when God is its portion
the richest valley land handed out by lot

games.q: what's inside Psalm 16 — tap the pairs.
p: no land: God was their portion

s: 'the lines' in Psalm 16 are lines of poetry
they're measuring cords: the share of land that fell to you.
Peter quotes Psalm 16 in his sermon at Pentecost
in Acts 2, at Pentecost, he reads it of the resurrection.
scholars know exactly what michtam means
nobody's sure. a golden poem, a secret, an inscription: all guesses.

games.q: the land is divided by lot. your share is a rocky hillside, and your cousin got the valley. what does the psalmist say about his lines?
o: the lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places.
I'll trade for a better lot.
games.why: pleasant places, and a goodly heritage, because his real portion is God: "The LORD is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup."

practice: Think of where your lines have fallen, and pick just one pleasant place: a kitchen where people laugh, a walk you take, a chair by a window.
Picture its light and its sounds, and say quietly, this is mine, and it's good; if some of your lines fell on rocky ground, you don't have to pretend otherwise. If you pray, give thanks for it.

wordCard.voice: Pleasant places. In Psalm sixteen, where the measuring lines of a life have fallen, when God is its portion.

orig.note: Hebrew: cords, measuring lines. The lines that marked out each family's share of land.

carryVoice: Your line: a goodly heritage. The Levites got no field, and still had a portion. Day four hundred fourteen.
